lessons.title: Ruby scripts and command-line conventions
lessons.intro:
Ruby 3.x. Ruby executes scripts directly, and -e evaluates a short program. ARGV contains user arguments without the executable name. A file can be both a reusable definition and a script by guarding its entry point with __FILE__ == $PROGRAM_NAME. Keep normal output on stdout and diagnostics on stderr. ruby -c checks syntax; it does not execute the program or prove its behavior. The tutor shows commands as text, and does not run them.

lessons.title: Keyword arguments and block contracts
lessons.intro:
Ruby 3.x. Ruby 3 separates keyword arguments from positional hashes. Use ** to forward a keyword hash and & to forward a block. A required keyword documents a method contract; omitting it raises ArgumentError. block_given? allows a method to offer a default behavior when no block was supplied. Lambdas enforce their declared arity more strictly than ordinary procs. Read these call boundaries before attempting to repair a missing argument.

lessons.title: Duck typing and Ruby object protocols
lessons.intro:
Ruby 3.x. Ruby code often asks whether an object responds to a useful message rather than requiring a particular class. each is the core protocol behind Enumerable; include adds its instance methods. When no block is supplied, enum_for can expose an Enumerator instead. to_s is a display conversion while inspect targets diagnostics. respond_to? helps inspect a public capability, but cannot guarantee that a method will succeed for every input.

Read each snippet, identify its effect, then complete a fragment. Examples are independent unless stated otherwise. Snippets may omit surrounding entry points and standard imports; displayed code is never executed by the tutor.

  return enum_for(:each) unless block_given?
  yield ${n}
 end
end

lessons.title: Standard-library tests and recoverable boundaries
lessons.intro:
Ruby 3.x. A useful script keeps transformation methods separate from command-line input and output. Ruby ships standard-library tools such as JSON, while Test::Unit is distributed as a bundled gem on common Ruby installations and may need installation separately. These lessons read tests without requiring a testing framework in the tutor. An assertion checks an expected outcome; a test for an exception should identify the specific failure. Rescue at a boundary where the application can decide how to respond.
